title: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership
excerpt: Meta on Monday announced plans to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
title_en: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership
excerpt_en: Meta on Monday announced plans to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
content_en:
Nvidia has said it will invest $3 billion in Meta after the social media and AI giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

The announcement said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.

## Nvidia deepens Meta ties

Nvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month.

"AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.

"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents."

"We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Both companies' shares were flat in premarket trading on Tuesday.

Nvidia has been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom, investing in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

title: Silicon Valley AI political groups turn on each other in the 2026 election
excerpt: AI political groups are spending millions in the 2026 election as Silicon Valley factions battle over regulation, safeguards and state authority.
title_en: Silicon Valley AI political groups turn on each other in the 2026 election
excerpt_en: AI political groups are spending millions in the 2026 election as Silicon Valley factions battle over regulation, safeguards and state authority.
content_en:
Silicon Valley's bid to dominate artificial intelligence politics has devolved into a fight with itself.

With one week until the midterm election, political groups favoring faster AI development and lighter, more uniform rules have spent roughly $8 million in general-election congressional races, besting groups pushing for stronger safeguards and more room for states to regulate that have spent about $6.9 million, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 20.

In Florida's 25th Congressional District, that split has produced a direct face-off. During the primary, Think Big, an affiliate of Leading the Future, the main super PAC network pushing faster AI development and lighter regulation, spent $310,000 supporting Democrat Jared Moskowitz, whose district changed after Florida redrew its congressional map ahead of the 2026 election. On the other side, Defending Our Values, a super PAC favoring stricter safety guardrails and state-level authority, dropped almost $857,000 to boost Republican Scott Singer and an additional $740,000 to keep one of his primary opponents from being elected.

Now, Moskowitz and Singer face off in the general election.

It's a microcosm of the breakdown in Silicon Valley's bid to build a unified AI political machine. Both sides favor AI innovation and agree on the need for guardrails, but they remain locked in a costly tug-of-war over which candidates to back — and which will best align with their preferred deployment speed, regulatory reach and balance of state power.

Electing more allies could give either camp an edge in shaping AI policy in the next Congress, even as the feud risks weakening Silicon Valley's clout.

"Everyone supports some form of regulation. It's just a debate about how much," said Bruce Freed, president and co-founder of the nonpartisan Center for Political Accountability and a former chief investigator for the Senate banking committee. "Money is flowing in all directions to be in the driver's seat of what happens."

CNBC identified federal committees aligned with each camp and totaled their FEC-reported independent expenditures supporting or opposing congressional candidates. The analysis excludes state races and nonprofit advocacy spending.

## The crypto playbook

This was not the plan. The model was cryptocurrency.

Fairshake and its affiliated pro-crypto super PACs, backed by Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz, spent more than $130 million during the 2024 election cycle, according to FEC filings. Candidates it supported won 53 of 58 races, a 91% success rate, according to crypto publication CoinDesk.

AI investors took note. In August 2025, Leading the Future launched with more than $100 million in commitments from tech heavyweights including Andreessen Horowitz, OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, and Perplexity and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale.

Co-led by Josh Vlasto, who worked for Fairshake last election cycle, the network deployed a Democratic PAC, Think Big, and a Republican PAC, American Mission, to support candidates aligned with faster AI development and opposition to a patchwork of state regulations.

The message was clear: Back AI's agenda or risk millions being spent against you.

"The AI industry announced last year that they were going to rerun the crypto industry playbook by coming in swinging with oodles of money in order to bully lawmakers into submission," said Sacha Haworth, founder and executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit watchdog that advocates for stronger regulation of Big Tech and AI.

At first, it worked. In the cycle's first major primaries in March, three candidates heavily backed by American Mission — Jessica Steinmann in Texas, Chris Gober in Texas and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina — won their Republican contests after the group spent more than $500,000 supporting each, according to FEC filings.

But a rival infrastructure was already taking shape. Anthropic committed $20 million to Public First Action in February and another $20 million in July, giving the safeguards camp a major financial backer. Anthropic says its money is restricted to policy and public education and cannot fund candidate elections. Still, separately funded super PACs tied to Public First Action have spent millions advancing similar priorities.

The clash burst into view in New York’s 12th District Democratic primary. Think Big spent $8.3 million, according to FEC filings, trying to defeat state Assemblymember Alex Bores, who authored major state AI safety legislation. The Anthropic-backed Jobs and Democracy PAC countered with about $15 million to support him, while allied safety groups spent millions more, according CNBC's analysis.

Think Big and Jobs and Democracy spent a combined $23.3 million, about 40% of the two camps' primary spending nationwide, according to the analysis.

Bores ultimately lost to Micah Lasher, 39% to 35%, giving Think Big a tactical victory.

"They helped light a flame under the backlash that's now fueling so much of the midterm elections," Haworth said. "The race showed that spending against safety-first candidates could now trigger a counterattack from within the industry itself."

## The money slows

The fight has carried into the general election, but the pace of spending plummeted.

Safeguards-focused groups have spent $825,000 this fall opposing two Republicans who benefited from Leading the Future-aligned spending during the primaries, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings. The two races alone account for more than one-sixth of the safeguards camp's general-election opposition spending.

Guardrails Alliance reported spending $412,500 apiece, according to FEC filings, against Republican House candidates Jay Feely in Arizona and Aaron Flint in Montana, both of whom benefited from Leading the Future-aligned spending in their primaries. It also reported about $412,000 against Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez in California, whom Leading the Future endorsed but did not report spending to support, according to CNBC's analysis.

"The big AI groups still believe that their money can help influence elections even if it's just a couple in November," Haworth said.

Yet the overall flow of AI campaign money has slowed since the primaries.

Leading the Future's network reported roughly $26 million in primary independent expenditures, compared with about $8 million in general-election races. Safeguards-focused groups reported about $32.1 million in primary spending and $6.9 million in general-election contests. The groups reported another roughly $5.5 million in runoff and special-election spending.

Combined, about 74% of the roughly $78.5 million they have spent on federal candidates this cycle went toward primary races, according to CNBC's analysis.

Some of that decline reflects the smaller universe of competitive November races. But the slowdown has coincided with AI becoming a more difficult political sell.

A new CNBC All-America Economic Survey found 52% of registered voters said companies should pause development of advanced AI until Congress passes regulations, compared with 32% who favored moving ahead. Sixty-three percent said they would oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home.

“When evaluating risk versus reward right now, the backlash is just too big,” said Freed, of the Center for Political Accountability.

“AI executives and groups spent heavily in the primaries, so they likely achieved what they set out to do in most races. At this point, there's no real downside to scaling back,” Freed said.

Some major donors have gone further.

The Brockmans gave $25 million to Leading the Future. But amid objections from OpenAI employees to the group's tactics, OpenAI's chief strategy officer acknowledged internally that the company was taking "reputational hits," according to Semafor.

content_en:
# Anthropic uses its IPO letter to renew its pledge that Claude will never show ads

**Anthropic promises once more to keep ads out of Claude's chat.** In its IPO filing cover letter, the company explains why it is passing on a potential massive revenue stream that funds much of the internet. "People bring some of their most important work and most personal questions to Claude, and we want Claude's only incentive to be giving them a helpful answer," Anthropic writes, adding that "once advertising becomes part of a company's revenue targets, the pressure to optimize for engagement tends to grow. We have chosen not to introduce that pressure into Claude." Anthropic previously criticized rival ChatGPT for running chat ads, warning they could be more manipulative than traditional ads.

The ad ban falls under the letter's second category, which puts company values above profit. As another example, Anthropic cites Claude Mythos Preview, then its most powerful model, whose advanced cyber capabilities posed high risks. Adding extra safeguards delayed its release as Claude Fable 5, costing Anthropic revenue and market share against rivals, while the company also gave cyber defenders about $100 million in free Claude credits. As future models grow stronger, Anthropic expects more decisions that forego maximum profit.

title: Anthropic's IPO is risky business
excerpt: Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.
excerpt_en: Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.
content_en:
Anthropic's much-anticipated initial public offering is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.

More than 90 pages of Anthropic's IPO prospectus, revealed Monday, center on the AI lab's multitude of corporate risk factors, many of which go beyond the kinds of boilerplate scenarios typically found in corporate filings.

From the end of humanity to the company's current clash with the Trump administration, Anthropic's IPO document underscores how one of the most well-capitalized startups in history foresees the future of its operations.

## Anthropic's IPO gets existential

The Claude maker's risks include a laundry list of ways its models can cause harm, including potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

It's imperative for Anthropic to emphasize AI safety because failure to do so could adversely affect its "brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," the filing said. But fierce competition, market pressure and stakeholder expectations make the task of safely developing and implementing bleeding-edge foundation models particularly challenging.

Anthropic can't guarantee that its AI safety efforts will be adequate, as the technology's inherent complexity makes it difficult for the company to plan for and predict every potential scenario.

## Feeling the data center heat

The public's souring position on data centers poses a major risk for Anthropic, which relies on an ever-expanding portfolio of state-of-the-art computing facilities to train and maintain its prized foundation models.

And with the midterm elections approaching, the tech industry's massive data center buildout has turned political, with lawmakers in 16 states considering moratoriums, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

"Opposition to data center development has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," the filing said.

## Power problems

Anthropic's future success depends not only on building giant data centers, but also on the electrical and related power infrastructure needed to juice those computing facilities.

The lack of "sufficient electrical power" across the nation and world poses big risks to Anthropic and its rivals, the filing notes. Even if energy becomes more readily available through "on-site natural gas-fired generation," that power could become more expensive with so much demand, the filing said.

## The kids are not alright

Rivals like OpenAI and Meta have come under fire from lawmakers and plaintiffs' attorneys over allegations that the design and implementation of their AI models and apps have fostered certain child-safety-related harms. Meta recently agreed to pay roughly $17 billion in a settlement with multiple state AGs in litigation involving child mental health and technology addiction.

Thus far, Anthropic has largely avoided scrutiny, but the filing noted that the company could potentially face its own legal headaches. Based on its terms of service, minors aren't allowed to access Claude and related products.

Anthropic knows it has work to do protecting children "as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access."

## No slowpokes

The company calling to pace the frontier also says it's a risk to move too slowly.

Anthropic needs to keep racing and needs the rest of the business world to keep up. If companies curb their AI spending, Anthropic could feel the burn.

"If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected," the filing says.

The prospectus also cites reduced demand for frontier models as a risk. Customers might find that lower-cost models work fine for them and that "incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost," instead choosing cheaper, or open-source alternatives.

content_en:
# OpenAI's partner content arrives in ChatGPT pre-summarized while the rest of the web gets raw scraps

**Content from OpenAI's licensing partners appears to flow into ChatGPT through a dedicated pipeline that gives it priority over the rest of the web.**That's the finding of an analysis by David Konitzny, a GEO researcher at Berlin-based startup Peec AI. Of three configured news engines, only one called "labrador" populates a field named "provider." Through that field, Konitzny identified 12 publishers with 43 domains, including Condé Nast, Hearst, Axel Springer, News Corp, Reuters, and AP. Beyond news, the pipeline also feeds recipes, product reviews, and buying guides from sites like Allrecipes, Tom's Guide, and Welt into the chatbot.

ChatGPT doesn't fetch partner pages live. Instead, it receives them as pre-generated summaries, while regular web pages arrive as raw text snippets. In the prompt, partner entries are placed ahead of all web results. For ranked lists, the summaries name 70 percent of entries in positions 1 through 3 but only 23 percent of those in positions 7 through 10, according to 1,000 cases Konitzny analyzed.

OpenAI had promised partners more prominent placement in ChatGPT back in 2024, and a study from Hamburg later found Springer media appearing far more often in the web interface than through the API. But even partners don't always get cited correctly.

title_en: Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push
excerpt_en: Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data.
content_en:
Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1.

It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year.

## China and the US lead

The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested.

The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics, a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics, which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round.

In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI, which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain.

Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics, which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence.

## Building out the data and model layer

“We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen, co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord, a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month.

The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said.

Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen.

We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted.

## More winners

Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others.

Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year.

“There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen.

title: Nvidia backs Indian startup helping companies run AI models with fewer GPUs
excerpt: Simplismart says its annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold in six months, with the U.S. accounting for more than half its revenue.
title_en: Nvidia backs Indian startup helping companies run AI models with fewer GPUs
excerpt_en: Simplismart says its annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold in six months, with the U.S. accounting for more than half its revenue.
content_en:
As the AI boom strains computing capacity, Nvidia has backed Indian startup Simplismart in a $14 million funding round, betting on software that helps companies run AI models more efficiently and, in some cases, with fewer GPUs.

Nvidia participated in the all-primary Series B round alongside Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax, with Dallas Venture Capital leading the investment. The deal values the four-year-old startup at about $100 million, including the new funding.

Companies are nowadays spending heavily on GPUs to power AI applications, but running those models reliably and economically at scale remains a challenge. Different workloads demand distinct trade-offs between speed, cost, and performance. Deploying and operating AI models to meet business requirements often also requires complex adjustments. Simplismart says its software automates much of that work, tailoring how models run on existing computing infrastructure instead of requiring customers to manage those configurations themselves.

“Nobody actually needs the fastest or the cheapest inference,” Amritanshu Jain (pictured above, left), co-founder and CEO of Simplismart, said in an interview. He added that companies instead need to run AI models at speeds and costs that make sense for their specific applications.

Simplismart’s software sits between AI models and the computing infrastructure they run on and adjusts how models are deployed and managed to meet customers’ requirements. It says it can optimize factors such as how quickly a model responds, how many requests it handles, and how much computing power it consumes, helping companies get more out of their existing GPU stack.

The Bengaluru-based startup offers companies a way to deploy and run AI models through its own platform or within their existing cloud and on-premises infrastructure. It also provides tools to fine-tune models, automatically scale computing resources as demand changes, and monitor performance. Additionally, Simplismart allows cloud providers build and operate their own AI inference services on GPU infrastructure using its software.

Simplismart says it helped AI video-generation platform InVideo cut its GPU serving costs by 56% using its software. The startup also works with AI video companies HeyGen and Higgsfield, as well as enterprise AI startup Ema, among others. Moreover, Indian cloud provider Yotta uses Simplismart’s technology to power the serverless AI inference service within its Shakti Studio platform.

Simplismart’s annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months to an eight-figure sum, Jain told TechCrunch. The figure is based on recent customer usage rather than contracted recurring revenue and excludes revenue passed through to infrastructure providers, the company said. He did not disclose the exact figure.

More than half of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the U.S., despite the startup having more customers in India, Jain said.

Alongside its investment, Nvidia has been working with Simplismart on technical integrations, including around its Dynamo inference software, Jain told TechCrunch. The collaboration involves Simplismart’s engineers and Nvidia’s solutions architects, while Nvidia has also helped introduce the startup to potential customers and partners, Jain stated.

Interestingly, the investment presents an apparent paradox as Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI chips, is backing software that can help companies run some workloads with fewer GPUs. Jain, however, argued that making AI inference more efficient could ultimately benefit Nvidia by making its hardware more attractive to customers and encouraging wider adoption of AI applications.

Simplismart is serving customers in an increasingly crowded market for AI inference software, competing with offerings from Nvidia itself, as well as major cloud providers and hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. A growing number of startups are also developing tools to make AI models faster and cheaper to run as there is growing demand in this segment, driven by rising demand for AI applications and the need to make better use of expensive GPU resources.

“Where we tend to win is where people have to be more stringent on their SLAs \[service-level agreements\] and TCO \[total cost of ownership\],” Jain said, referring to demanding performance requirements and tight cost constraints. Unlike rivals that offer preset options for faster or cheaper inference, Simplismart aims to find a balance tailored to each customer’s needs, he said.

Founded in 2022 by former Oracle engineer Jain and former Google engineer Devansh Ghatak (pictured above, right), Simplismart grew out of the pair’s experience building and deploying machine-learning systems. The two met while studying at BITS Pilani, and the startup now employs 58 people, Jain said.

Simplismart plans to use the new funding to expand its presence in the U.S., grow its team, and invest further in developing its inference software. Jain told TechCrunch that the U.S. remains a key market for the startup as it looks to build on its existing customer base there.

The funding announcement follows a report by Indian English daily The Economic Times that Simplismart was in talks to raise $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $300 million to $400 million. Asked about the report, Jain declined to comment, saying the startup was not actively fundraising. He added that the Series B was closed and would not be extended.

content_en:
# OpenAI's Ted Sanders shares a rule of thumb for picking the right GPT-model

**OpenAI's Ted Sanders has categorized the new GPT-6.1 Terra and explained how the company names its language models.** According to Sanders, model performance is multidimensional. A model that's great at math won't automatically be good at jokes. Still, most performance gaps come down to one variable: model size. Sanders says OpenAI's model names are difficult to simplify because model size, reasoning effort, and multi-agent systems are distinct dimensions. Combining them into a single "IQ score" would obscure details.

And size doesn't explain everything. Newer, smaller models can outperform older, larger ones through better training data or improved architectures. GPT-6.1 Terra is likely better than the larger Astra at technical communication and roughly matches it in image processing and computer use at a much lower price point, but falls short in most other areas, Sanders says. "If you care about quality only, pick Astra. If you're a bit price sensitive, pick Sol. If you're very price sensitive, pick Terra or Luna."

# Meta gets $3 billion from Nvidia and plans to spend more on Nvidia chips

**Nvidia is buying into its customer Meta, which plans to run more of its AI agents on Nvidia hardware.** Nvidia is investing $3 billion in Meta's planned equity offering, the Wall Street Journal reports. In the same announcement, the two companies said they would expand their partnership around Meta's AI product Muse. Meta plans to use more Nvidia infrastructure for its next generation of AI agents, including Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs.

Meta wants to raise up to $95 billion through stock offerings to pay for its AI infrastructure buildout. According to CNBC, AMD and Broadcom also signaled nonbinding interest in buying up to $5 billion in Meta shares combined.

The deal fits a pattern investors have been arguing about for months. Nvidia gives money to customers like OpenAI, which then use it to build data centers packed with Nvidia chips. Critics call this circular financing and warn that it could hide how much real demand exists.

excerpt: Scaling AI agents requires treating them like employees in regulated roles, with written rules, clearly defined responsibilities and a named human manager accountable for their performance. Guest author Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered, tells companies they should start with tasks governed by established rules, adjust autonomy to each workflow’s risks, and regularly review results before expandin
title_en: Your AI Agents Need A Chief Operating Officer, Too
excerpt_en: Scaling AI agents requires treating them like employees in regulated roles, with written rules, clearly defined responsibilities and a named human manager accountable for their performance. Guest author Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered, tells companies they should start with tasks governed by established rules, adjust autonomy to each workflow’s risks, and regularly review results before expandin
content_en:
A landlord in California has 21 days after a resident moves out to return the security deposit or send an itemized list of deductions. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it.

I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered, we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to.

Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years.

Gartner, meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.

Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review.

Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling.

## Start with work that already has a rulebook

The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement.

Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified.

Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls.

McKinsey‘s most recent State of AI research found that the small group of companies seeing significant bottom-line returns from AI, about 6% of respondents, were nearly 3x as likely to have fundamentally redesigned their workflows.

In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either.

## Set autonomy by workflow

Tech execs I speak with often ask whether an AI system is autonomous, as if that were a fixed property of the product. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches.

At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. For instance, a reminder to a vendor whose certificate expires next month can go out automatically. A response to a resident who has requested an emotional support animal never does.

A useful exercise for any leadership team is to list every workflow an agent will touch and ask one question about each: If this action is wrong, how long until we find out, and what will it have cost by then? Quick detection and low cost earn an agent more room.

## Give every agent an owner with a name

Earlier in my career I learned that every automated credit decision eventually had to be explained to a customer, a regulator, or both. The model did it was never an acceptable answer.

That still holds, except agents now act more often and across more systems than any underwriting model did.

So every agent at our company has a person ultimately responsible, the same way a team or a budget does. That person reviews its error log, decides when to widen or narrow its autonomy, and answers for it.

Ownership also heads off a quieter problem. When several teams launch agents independently, nobody sees where those agents contradict one other.

## Where the constraint actually sits

In today’s marketplace, it’s inevitable that the models will keep improving. A company’s clarity about who decides what will not improve on its own. Gartner’s cancellation forecast reflects that: Most agent projects that fail will do so because nobody defined the value or controlled the risk, and both of those are management problems.

For decision-makers heading into 2027, my advice is to treat each agent the way you would treat a new employee in a regulated role. Write down its rules, limit its scope, and assign it a manager who checks its work and discusses its performance.

Companies that do this will be able to give agents more responsibility over time, because they will have the evidence to justify it. Businesses that skip it will spend 2027 explaining why their software did something nobody approved.

*Rick Folgmann is chief operating officer at Get Covered, an insurance technology company that provides cost-effective property coverage with just a few clicks. He has more than 25 years of executive leadership experience in the financial and insurance industries.*

title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
excerpt: As agents go mainstream, some publishers are hoping that people will pay for content tailor-made for AI—not humans.
title_en: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
excerpt_en: As agents go mainstream, some publishers are hoping that people will pay for content tailor-made for AI—not humans.
content_en:
Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a morning briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.

Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.

“I'm kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.

Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.

“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. ”We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.

Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.

Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.

What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.

“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”

At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.

“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.

The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger-and-acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.

Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’s reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.

While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.

Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.

Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.

Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.

Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.

“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you're telling,” Shipper says. “And there's always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.

“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.

As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?

Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.

Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’s chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don't want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that's something that's already benefiting us.”

But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.

Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.

Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”

Murphy says that Axios’s starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.

content_en:
**Querio**, a London-based analytics platform for data teams and their AI agents, has launched today with €4.48 million ($5 million) in total funding.

Its investors include BMW i Ventures, which led the company’s Seed financing, alongside LAUNCH, the fund run by Jason Calacanis, Haatch Ventures, Araya, Forum Ventures, and Secways.

*“Companies want to use AI with their data, but they need to trust the answer. Querio lets data teams hand more of the work to AI agents while a person stays in charge of every change that reaches the business,”* said **Javier Bonilla**, co-founder and CTO at Querio.

Founded in 2024 by Rami Abi Habib (CEO) and Bonilla (CTO), Querio is an AI analytics platform that helps data teams give the whole company consistent answers in the AI tools it already uses. It keeps a company’s reports, definitions, and analysis in the data team’s GitHub and claims to give business users consistent answers in Claude, ChatGPT, and Slack, with the data team reviewing every change.

According to the company, it was launched to address the growing challenge of keeping answers consistent across tools as employees turn to AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT for business questions.

It says that when each tool uses a different version of the company’s numbers, people get conflicting answers, and data teams spend their time reconciling them instead of doing new work.

Querio claims to give data teams one place to define what the company’s numbers mean, and keeps that work in the team’s own GitHub rather than locked inside a vendor’s product.

*“For thirty years, analytics tools have kept a company’s logic inside the vendor’s product, where it’s hard to move and hard for AI to work with. Now everyone is asking data questions in Claude, Slack and wherever else they work, and they get three different revenue numbers. We built Querio so the data team owns that logic, and every AI tool in the company answers from it,”* said **Abi Habib**, co-founder and CEO of Querio.

The UK startup highlighted that business users can ask questions in Claude, ChatGPT or Slack and get the same answer each time. It further notes that when the business changes, Querio’s AI agent updates the affected reports and definitions, and the data team approves each change before anyone sees it.

“Say sales renames a field in the CRM. The revenue dashboard breaks, the Slack bot says no deals closed last week and Claude gives a third number. With Querio, the agent spots the change, fixes everything that depends on it and sends the data team one update to approve. After that, every tool gives the same answer,” Abi Habib added.

Querio is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA- and GDPR-compliant. It also said it does not train on customer data and maintains no-training and no-storage agreements with its AI model providers. It works with companies including OpenVPN and agree.com.

title: I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
excerpt: I ranked six AI agents—from Meta’s Muse to Anthropic’s Claude Duet—on how well they completed basic tasks.
title_en: I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
excerpt_en: I ranked six AI agents—from Meta’s Muse to Anthropic’s Claude Duet—on how well they completed basic tasks.
content_en:
Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.

As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.

Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.

It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.

Each agent differs slightly in price and function. **Muse** is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. **Instinct** is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s **Dots** are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s **Gemini Spark** is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s **Grok Bot** costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s **Claude Duet** costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.

OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.

## What Exactly Is an AI Agent?

If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.

Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.

## The Rubric

I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.

This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.

Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.

## Morning Briefing

On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.

I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.

The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.

**Gemini Spark:**5/5. A conversational headline that identifies a core tension online.

*Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.*

**Claude Duet:**4/5. Another interesting and timely pitch.

*ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.*

**Muse:**3/5. Not bad, but not

*that*strong.

*I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.*

**Dots:**2/5. More evergreen than newsy.

*This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.*

**Grok Bot:**1/5. Old news.

*Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.*

**Instinct:**1/5. A bland and hard-to-measure experiment.

*I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.*

## Lunch Time

Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whiche

content_en:
### SAP advances its autonomous enterprise push with smarter, governed Joule agents

SAP SE today announced a set of artificial intelligence innovations at its annual TechEd conference for developers, enhancing its Joule assistant solutions and Business AI Platform, including tabular data foundation models.

New capabilities in Joule Work will help AI agents become more efficient and interoperate with open protocols. In this case, the Model Context Protocol and Agent 2 Agent allow Joule, the company’s agentic AI assistant, to gather context, make decisions and execute multistep business workflows across the enterprise, while also bringing in third-party data or services.

However, every time an agent goes to work, it needs to be governed by a central authority just like an employee; it needs access and it must execute on tools with permissions. “Open protocols need governed doors,” Ted Way, vice president and chief product officer of SAP business AI product engineering, told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Way explained that SAP would like customers’ own agents to collaborate with its business agents across company systems. The proposition is that opening those interconnections also requires a controlled entry point where organizations can enforce and oversee activity. This is where a new orchestration layer will come in, enabling assistants and agents to invoke Joule Agents through a governed gateway.

In addition, a recent update will allow agents to trigger n8n workflows, an important connector through Joule Studio. N8n is a node-based workflow automation platform that connects different apps and uses deterministic automation; this means that AI agents can trigger it, but unlike generative AI, n8n uses event-based and trigger-based logic for decision-making. It cannot hallucinate; it is not random and will follow exact rules from start to finish.

That means n8n is suitable for highly regulated or sensitive work that depends on exact needs.

“It needs to do these five steps in this order exactly like this every single time,” Way explained, so in that case, n8n is the go-to.

SAP’s approach combines flexible, natural-language agentic triggers with a prescribed workflow. An agent may help determine when it is needed, while compliance-sensitive procedures can still require an exact sequence of steps.

### SAP builds on cloud data to ground the autonomous enterprise

The company today announced the expansion of SAP Business Data Cloud Ontology Manager in SAP Data Cloud, or BDC, to provide an AI-native authoring experience for businesses by giving agents an understanding of how applications relate to one another. It does so by defining relationships between company facts, allowing agents to reason more accurately and make decisions across enterprises.

SAP’s acquisition of Reltio, recently announced at SAP Connect, brings on board multidomain data management to BDC. That helps unify customer, supplier and product records across SAP and third-party systems into trusted data products for applications and agents.

The new product is designed to complement the company’s existing Knowledge Graph, which provides rich business context from SAP data.

Additionally, the company said, it’s expanding its lakehouse capabilities with Dremio, another acquisition, by adding native support for Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris and a high-performance, federated query engine that enables unified data access without moving or copying data.

### Bringing AI models to tables

“Not every enterprise problem is a language problem,” Way said, explaining that although much of the AI approach has focused on natural language, much business data is stored in tables.

To handle this, SAP announced its latest tabular AI model, SAP-RPT-2.0, which expands beyond classification and regression to support anomaly and outlier detection, providing AI-powered analysis through embeddings. It will give multitable capabilities to reduce manual engineering and deliver faster, deeper insights from structured data.

The company also launched a new SAP-RPT-TS model, which will help customers predict values across time-indexed metrics for key forecasting. It uses SAP Business Planning without custom business machine learning, allowing less technical users to deploy the model on their systems.

In a partnership with Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., SAP announced it’s deploying SAP-RPT on the International Space Station. The aim is to assist with predicting issues before failures escalate, reconstruct missing sensor values from historical data, and generate explainable mission health reports for astronauts and ground teams, all without sending data back to Earth before analysis.

content_en:
### Cisco Partner Summit: Five insights that will define the channel in the AI era

For most of its 30-year history, Cisco Partner Summit has focused on how partners sell Cisco Systems Inc. technology. This year’s event in Vancouver was about something different: how partners make money in a world where the transaction is no longer the main event.

Cisco entered the event with tremendous momentum, as its stock was up more than 50% over the past 12 months. Tim Coogan (pictured), senior vice president of global partner sales, told the 2,000 partners in attendance that channel bookings accounted for about 90% of Cisco’s total in fiscal 2026 and that global channel growth was just over 17%. Chief Executive Chuck Robbins called fiscal 2026 “the absolute best year that Cisco’s ever had.” Good years can mask structural change, though, and the announcements in Vancouver signal a real rethink of how value moves through Cisco’s partner ecosystem.

Here are my five takeaways that should matter to Cisco partners.

### Influence now counts, not just transactions

The most significant change in Vancouver may also be the least flashy. Ecosystem Deal Registration gives advisers, consultants and developers formal credit for helping Cisco win a deal, even when they don’t execute it. This group of partners hasn’t received the same level of attention as traditional reseller partners, yet they are now critical in the AI era.

Today, that credit takes the form of marketing support and promotion alongside Cisco sellers. Starting next spring, preferred advisers and developers will be eligible for referral incentives. Cisco is also introducing dedicated Partner Value Indexes for advisors and developers, with a unified distributor index planned for 2027.

Coogan emphasized the importance of the change. “Our traditional programs were transaction-based,” he said during his portion of the keynote. “This is a unique way to bring the entire ecosystem of partners together into a single solution for the benefit of our customers.”

The data presented supports this change. Cisco cited Omdia research showing that customers rely on six to seven partners and pass through 28 moments of influence before buying. A program that pays only the partner holding the paper ignores most of what shapes the decision. The risk is channel conflict, and resellers will want proof that rewarding influence grows the pie rather than splitting it.

Robbins addressed the bumpiness of the Cisco 360 rollout and the company’s willingness to take corrective action. “We’re not perfect. We’ll screw it up, but we’ll fix it,” he said. This is a great example of his statement, and partners should continue to hold him to it.

### Cisco IQ turns services into the business

If one announcement could change partner economics, it would be Cisco IQ Partner Branded Support Standard. Partners can now deliver Cisco IQ under their own brand, through their own experts, with role-based access to customer installed bases, application programming interfaces, IT service management integrations, and a Model Context Protocol server.

“For too long, partners entered customer conversations without the same view as Cisco. That changes today,” said Liz Centoni, executive vice president and chief customer experience officer. “It’s their name, their customer relationship and their services practice. Cisco IQ is the engine. Partners are the business.”

Centoni presented several compelling proof points. More than 16,000 customers and nearly 20 million devices are now on Cisco IQ. Generali reduced the time to assess a single security advisory across 16,000 devices from four days to 10 minutes. Georgetown University transformed two months of manual renewal work into a 20-minute view.

On stage, Centoni gave an example that quantified the opportunity. In her example, a partner who walks in to refresh 75 switches books about $625,000 and walks away. A partner who starts with Cisco IQ, identifies uncovered devices, sells hardening services, designs the refresh, and then runs managed operations across all 175 switches can reach roughly $1.3 million over five years, including incentives. That’s 2.1 times the value. “Basic gives you the map. Standard and Signature give you the GPS,” she said.

Cisco is backing that with a $2,500 adoption incentive per onboarded customer, a 6% deal registration on Standard and Signature support, and a $1 million Builders Challenge for partners who create managed services on Cisco IQ. My take is that Cisco is moving partners from project revenue to recurring revenue, where valuation multiples are higher. Partners who sell Cisco IQ as a support add-on will miss the point.

### Mythos made modernization an emergency

For years, last-day-of-support conversations felt like a vendor pushing hardware. Robbins said as much. “When we used to stand up and talk about what we call LDOS (last day of support), people would go, ‘OK, that’s just the vendor trying to sell more equipment,’ and you would have been partially right,” he said. “Now the urgency of getting that equipment out of the infrastructure, equipment that can’t be patched and for which there are no spares, is a real emergency.”

Coogan provided the numbers that underscore the urgency. In 2018, more than two years passed between discovery and exploitation of a vulnerability. Last year, it was about three weeks. This year, it’s eight hours or less. Only 3% of partners named AI security a growth opportunity last year. This year, 33% did.

Cisco’s answer includes expanded Live Protect coverage, what it calls the industry’s first quantum-resilient Wi-Fi 7 access point, and Privileged Infrastructure Access, built with Teleport, which provides engineers and AI agents with short-lived, identity-bound access to routers and switches. Robbins framed the architecture this way: “If agents are operating across your infrastructure, the only common denominator they’re going to touch on a daily basis is the network.”

Robbins said only 8% of the installed base has been refreshed to Cisco’s new enterprise portfolio. But, in his words, customers are “overwhelmed.” The winning partners will present a phased plan outlining what to fix first and why. That’s an advisory skill, not a quoting skill.

### Margin follows the platform

Mark Patterson, executive vice president and chief financial officer, has attended Partner Summit for more than 20 years, but this was his first time onstage. His session was among the day’s most useful because he discussed what motivates partners most: money. On price increases, he said, “Raising prices is the absolute last resort for us.” He added that the Nov. 7 increase targets memory-intensive products rather than being spread “in a peanut butter fashion.”

His most important point concerned margin. “The big takeaway is that margin follows the platform,” Patterson said. “You might lead with compute, but then you add networking, security, Splunk and observability. That’s where you’ll drive much of the margin.”

The incentives align with that view. The program adds an extra 2% cross-sell bonus for expanding into new Cisco architectures, including Splunk. It increases the reward for annual contract value growth by 50%, doubles adoption incentives, and offers 12% deal registration for Supermicro systems sold as part of full-stack AI infrastructure. Coogan also made an unusual admission about Splunk. “We moved slower on Splunk than we wanted to, than we should have, and that changes this year and it changes now,” he said.

Patterson also highlighted Cisco Capital as underused, noting that “the margins are paid entirely up front,” which helps partners build larger deals for customers with heavy technical debt. The message is that thin-margin compute is the entry point, not where the profit lies.
